title: Of a monstrous child
paragraphs: This story shall stand by itself; I will leave it for physicians to discuss. Two days ago I saw a child whom two men and a nurse, who said they were the father, the uncle, and the aunt, were taking around to earn money by showing it, because it was so strange a creature. In every other respect it was of ordinary shape, could stand on its feet, walk and prattle much like other children of the same age, and so far had taken no other nourishment than the nurse's breasts; what they tried, in my presence, to put into its mouth, it merely chewed a little and spat out again without swallowing; its cry did seem a little odd and peculiar; it was just fourteen months old. Under the breast it was joined to another child, but without a head, and with the spine of the back without movement, the rest entire — one arm was shorter than the other, but had been broken by accident at birth. They were joined breast to breast, as though a smaller child were trying to throw its arms about the neck of a slightly bigger one. The joint and the thickness of the place where they were joined was no more than four fingers, or thereabouts, so that if you pushed the imperfect child upward, you could see the other one's navel below it, the joining being between the chest and the navel. The navel of the imperfect child could not be seen, but all the rest of its belly could; so that everything that was not joined of the imperfect one — arms, buttocks, thighs, and legs — hung dangling from the other and could reach down to mid-leg. The nurse also told us that it urinated through both bodies, and that the limbs of the other body were nourished, had feeling, and were in the same condition as those of the one she was suckling, except that they were shorter and smaller. This double body and several limbs attached to one head might be read as a favourable omen for the king, that he would keep the various parts of our state under the union of his laws; but for fear the event should prove otherwise, it is better to leave it alone, since with things already past there is no need for divination,
"Ut quum facts sunt, tum ad conjecturam aliqui interpretatione revocentur;"
["So as when they are come to pass, they may then by some interpretation be recalled to conjecture" — Cicero, De Divin., ii. 31.]
as it is said of Epimenides that he always prophesied backwards.

I have just seen a herdsman in Médoc, about thirty years old, with no sign of any genital parts; he has three holes through which he constantly passes water; he is bearded, has desire, and seeks contact with women.

Those whom we call monsters are not so to God, who sees in the immensity of his work the infinite forms he has comprehended in it; and it is to be believed that this figure that astonishes us is related to some other figure of the same kind unknown to man. From his all-wisdom nothing proceeds but what is good, common, and regular; but we do not see the order and connection:
"Quod crebro videt, non miratur, etiamsi, cur fiat, nescit. Quod ante non vidit, id, si evenerit, ostentum esse censet."
["What he often sees he does not admire, though he be ignorant how it comes to pass. When a thing happens he never saw before, he thinks that it is a portent." — Cicero, De Divin., ii. 22.]

Whatever falls out contrary to custom we call contrary to nature, but nothing whatsoever is contrary to her. Let this universal and natural reason expel the error and astonishment that novelty brings with it.
